newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian palmolein imports set to rise in Sept-Oct.
newsitem.headline: Indian palmolein imports set to rise in Sept-Oct.

text.p: India is expected to buy about 350,000 tonnes of palmolein in September and October, but imports would taper off from November with the arrival of the new crop, traders and officials said on Tuesday.
"Imports of about 350,000 tonnes of palmolein are expected during September and October," G.K. Sood, chief executive of the Vanaspati Manufacturers Association of India, told Reuters.
Sood said the lean domestic period coupled with the coming festival season had driven imports in the past few months.
O.P. Goenka, president of the Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT), said India was expected to import around 200,000 tonnes of palmolein in September and 150,000 tonnes in October.
India imported 560,000 tonnes of edible oil between June and August.
India's domestic stocks are tightest between July and October, and demand peaks in the Hindu festival months of September and October.
Officials estimated India's total edible oil imports in 1995/96 (Nov-Oct) at between 1.25 and 1.4 million tonnes compared to 700,000 tonnes in the previous year.

"Probably 1.0-to-1.2 million tonnes of edible oil has already been imported, and I am expecting 1.4 million tonnes in the current year," said O.P. Goenka, president of the Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT).
Sood projected edible oil imports in 1995/96 at 1.25 milion to 1.3 million tonnes.
Goenka attributed the spurt in imports to increased per capita consumption of edible oil to 7.5-8.0 kg per annum from 6.5-7.0 kg two years ago.
India produces about 6.5 million tonnes of edible oil annually. Its oilseeds output has been virtually stagnant at 22 million tonnes over the past few years.
Goenka said a steady flow of imports had prevented any sharp increase in domestic edible oil prices despite the shrinking local supplies.
Navinbhai Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd, said the industry was still estimating the size of the new crop due in November.
"Imports will dip from November onwards because the new crop will come. In the absence of clear estimates importers will not make long-term commitments," he said.
